text: The Gospels record that Jesus healed a man born blind, and the account is evaluated differently depending on one's methodological starting point. Those who approach the text with a presumption against supernatural causation may interpret the healing as a symbolic narrative or as a psychosomatic recovery, while those who allow for divine action may regard it as a genuine miracle. Neither interpretation can be established or excluded by historical method alone, and the question ultimately turns on one's philosophical commitments regarding the possibility of divine intervention in the natural order.

Whether the virginal conception of Jesus should be understood as a historical event or as a theological interpretation of Jesus's significance expressed through the narrative conventions of the time is a question on which scholars of equal erudition and good faith have reached different conclusions. Raymond E. Brown, in his comprehensive study The Birth of the Messiah, concluded that the historicity of the virginal conception cannot be proven or disproven by the tools available to the historian, and that the decision to affirm or reject it depends on one's prior judgements about the reliability of the infancy narratives and the possibility of miraculous events more broadly.

The resurrection of Jesus is the central claim of the New Testament, and assessments of its historicity vary considerably. Those who argue for its historicity point to the early date of the tradition Paul cites in 1 Corinthians 15, the empty tomb, the transformation of the disciples from fearful fugitives to bold proclaimers, and the emergence of the church in the very city where Jesus was executed. Those who argue against it point to the discrepancies among the Gospel accounts, the possibility that the disciples experienced hallucinations arising from bereavement, and the methodological principle that historians cannot invoke supernatural causes. Both positions involve complex judgements about the reliability of the sources, the nature of the experiences that generated the resurrection faith, and the philosophical assumptions that historians bring to their work.

The nature miracles of Jesus — the stilling of the storm, the walking on water, the feeding of the multitude — have been assessed along a range of interpretative possibilities. Some scholars regard them as historical events in which Jesus exercised divine power over the created order; others interpret them as symbolic narratives crafted by the early church to express Christological convictions in narrative form; still others seek naturalistic explanations compatible with modern scientific understanding. Each approach entails its own methodological commitments and yields different conclusions, and the state of the evidence does not compel the adoption of any one position to the exclusion of the others.

The exorcisms performed by Jesus are recorded in all three Synoptic Gospels and are multiply attested across independent sources. Interpretations of these accounts range from the traditional view that Jesus actually expelled malevolent spiritual beings, to the social-scientific view that Jesus addressed psychosomatic conditions using the culturally available idiom of the time, to the critical view that the exorcism stories are later legendary developments. Each interpretation makes distinct claims about the nature of the sources, the cultural context of first-century Palestine, and the limits of historical enquiry, and there is no scholarly consensus on which interpretation best accounts for all the available data.

The transfiguration narrative in the Synoptic Gospels is read by some scholars as a historical event — a genuine supernatural revelation witnessed by Peter, James, and John — and by others as a retrojection of resurrection appearance traditions into the earthly ministry, or as a symbolic literary composition drawing on Sinai and enthronement motifs. Each reading has been defended by scholars of standing, and the nature of the evidence is such that the question cannot be resolved on purely historical grounds. The interpretation one adopts is likely to depend on broader judgements about the Gospels' genre, the evangelists' methods of composition, and the possibility of supernatural events within the framework of critical historiography.

The gift of tongues at Pentecost, as narrated in Acts 2, is understood within traditional Christian theology as a miraculous endowment of the Spirit enabling the apostles to proclaim the gospel in languages they had not learned. Critical scholars have proposed alternative interpretations, including the possibility that Luke composed the account as a theological narrative about the reversal of Babel, or that the event reflects an early Christian experience of ecstatic speech that Luke has interpreted as xenolalia. Both approaches engage seriously with the text and its historical and literary context, and the question resists definitive resolution by the methods available to the historian.

The raising of Lazarus in John 11 is among the most dramatic miracle accounts in the New Testament, and its relationship to history has been debated extensively. Some scholars, such as C. H. Dodd and Raymond E. Brown, have treated the narrative as a historical tradition that John has developed for his theological purposes. Others, including Rudolf Bultmann, have argued that it is a 'sign-source' story that John has expanded into a narrative of Christological revelation. Still others regard it as a literary composition with no recoverable historical core. The scholarly debate reflects deep disagreements about the character of the Fourth Gospel, its relationship to the Synoptic tradition, and the appropriate criteria for assessing the historicity of the Gospel narratives.

The ascension of Jesus is presented in Luke and Acts as a visible departure from the Mount of Olives forty days after the resurrection. Interpretations of this account span a wide range. Some theologians regard the ascension as a historical event — the exaltation of Jesus's resurrected body into the divine realm. Others interpret it as a symbolic or liturgical narrative that expresses, in the spatial cosmology of the ancient world, the theological conviction that Jesus now exercises divine authority. Still others see it as Luke's literary device for closing the period of resurrection appearances and inaugurating the age of the Spirit. Each of these interpretations makes distinct claims about Luke's historiographical method, the nature of the resurrection body, and the relationship between theological truth and historical occurrence, and the textual and historical evidence does not, in the judgement of many scholars, decisively favour any one reading.

The accounts of angelic visitations in the infancy narratives — to Zechariah, Mary, Joseph, and the shepherds — are received by many Christians as records of genuine supernatural encounters. At the same time, scholars have observed that angelic annunciation scenes follow a recognisable literary pattern in both biblical and intertestamental literature, and that the evangelists may be employing this convention to emphasise the divine origin and significance of the events they narrate. Both the traditional and the literary-critical readings rest on careful attention to the texts and their backgrounds, and which reading one adopts is shaped by broader presuppositions about the relationship between literary form and historical referent.
